title: Highland Road noise, climate updates and waste strategy
subtitle: Also: Victoria Street design, road-works fee, drainage plan, Cambridge truck diversion, grass cutting and detours.
overview: The Planning and Works Committee heard a climate-aligned growth update, including the 2022 community emissions inventory, the corporate climate action plan, the corporate energy plan and a thermal energy strategy. These were received for information. Delegates described the region as not on track for its 2030 emissions target. Staff said the corporate climate action plan returns to Council in the fall.

The committee recommended guiding principles for the review of the Long-Term Waste Management Strategy {{vote:m7}}. Those principles are waste reduction, climate and energy collaboration, and a circular economy. It also recommended a refined Victoria Street design in Kitchener and a contract extension for final design. It recommended a new $5,000 developer fee for agreements on work on Regional roads, and approval of a drainage report for the East Side Lands.

On the Highland Road noise assessment, staff recommended that no noise wall is needed. After questions from councillors, the committee asked staff to look at a live noise study and report to Council on June 19. Nearby residents are still concerned about the modelled results.
The committee received the Cambridge truck diversion evaluation. It also discussed Snyder's Road parking, roadside grass cutting and long rural detours.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended three guiding principles for the Long-Term Waste Management Strategy review: reduce waste, collaborate on climate and energy targets, and align services with a circular economy {{vote:m7}}.

The committee recommended approving the refined design for Victoria Street between Fischer-Hallman Road and Lawrence Avenue in Kitchener, and a $245,320 plus HST extension to the design consultant's contract, for a total of $1,104,600 plus HST.

The committee recommended delegating signing authority for third-party infrastructure agreements on Regional roads to the relevant Commissioner, and adding a $5,000 plus HST developer fee to the fees by-law.
The committee recommended approving the Scoped Master Drainage Report for the Randall and Breslau Drains, to the extent it addresses matters of Regional interest.

The committee recommended that the Region enter into a revised Municipal Responsibility Agreement for upgrading a privately operated sewage treatment system in Floradale, to the satisfaction of the Regional Solicitor.
The committee recommended transferring the daylight triangles at Menno Street and Fountain Street North from the Region to the Township of Woolwich, with an indemnification agreement.

debate: Two delegates and several councillors questioned the Highland Road noise study. They said it relied on modelling rather than field measurements. They also said real speeds exceed the posted 60 km/h and that acceleration at the intersection and modified exhausts may not be captured. A delegate asked why the modelled levels differed so much from the earlier study.

Staff defended the modelling. They said the noise policy projects traffic and trucks ten years ahead, which cannot be measured today. They said the provincially approved model tends to over-predict noise, and that peak noise such as engine brakes would not be fixed by a wall twice as high. Staff said trees would give some mitigation but less than a wall.

Several councillors asked about speed, road design and a live test. One asked about the risk of a live test. Staff said there was none but it is not Regional policy, and no budget exists for it. Staff will report back on cost and on whether the old airport noise monitoring equipment is still available.

On climate, delegates said the region is not on track for a 50% cut by 2030 and urged more ambition. Councillors asked what faster action would mean for budgets and project choices. Staff said a faster pace would cost more and could be disruptive, and that the corporate climate action plan would set out the costs.

On the Cambridge truck diversion, councillors welcomed a reduction of about 60%. Staff said the goal is full diversion, which would likely need street redesign, since continued police enforcement is costly. One councillor said trucks had increased on a section outside the ban.
